opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think it was a gradual shift more than a single moment. As an undergrad I loved theory: algorithms, combinatorics, the elegance of proving something cleanly. But I kept finding myself drawn to problems where the mathematical structure actually connects to something that works in practice.

Machine learning was interesting to me because it sits right at that intersection. There's a lot of deep math underneath it, like linear algebra, approximation theory, and signal processing, but the field is also very empirical. You can have a beautiful idea, and then the real test is whether it trains well and scales. I found that tension really appealing.

When I started my PhD, I gravitated toward questions about how models represent and process sequences, especially long ones. That turned out to be a great fit for my background, because those questions have a lot of classical structure, like continuous-time systems, recurrences, and polynomial projections, that people in deep learning weren't fully exploiting. So a lot of my work since then, including state space models and eventually things like S4 and Mamba, has really been about taking that more principled, theoretical perspective and turning it into architectures that hold up empirically.

So I'd say I never fully left theory behind. I just found a place where that way of thinking could have a pretty direct impact.

r001.rationale: The response says Gu was drawn to problems connecting mathematical structure with practical results and found machine learning’s mix of theory and empirical work appealing. It does not say he cared more about machine learning’s research goals than theoretical computer science’s.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. Honestly, the path wasn't as deliberate as it might sound in hindsight. I started out loving math and theory, the kind of problems where you can prove something clean and know it's true. But somewhere during undergrad and into grad school, I kept noticing that the questions I found most exciting were the ones where the theory had to actually touch something real. Machine learning was this field where you could write down a beautiful idea on paper and then, a week later, see whether it worked or completely fell apart in practice. That feedback loop was addictive.

The other thing is that I came in a bit skeptical of deep learning, in the sense that a lot of it felt like alchemy. People would say "this architecture works" and nobody could really tell you why. For someone with a theory background, that's either frustrating or an invitation. I decided to treat it as an invitation. A lot of my early work, things like structured matrices and later the state space model line, really came from asking: can we understand what these models are computing in a principled way, and if we do, does that understanding let us design something better? Sometimes the answer was yes, which was incredibly motivating. Sometimes the answer was "the theory says this should work and it doesn't," which was humbling but also where the interesting problems live.

So I'd say what drew me over was less abandoning theory and more realizing that ML was a place where theory could matter, and where the gap between what we can prove and what we can build is still wide enough to spend a career in.

r001.rationale: The candidate says machine learning drew him because theory could be tested in practice and help improve models, but does not say he cared more about ML’s research goals than theoretical computer science’s.

astra-6.text: What drew me in was the gap between how well machine learning worked in practice and how much we could explain theoretically. Coming from theoretical computer science, I liked having precise questions and a framework for understanding why something works. Machine learning offered those kinds of questions, but with this additional opportunity to build something and see whether your ideas actually helped. That interaction between mathematical understanding and empirical results was really appealing to me.

r001.rationale: The response says the gap between machine learning’s practical success and theoretical explanation appealed to Albert Gu, along with testing ideas empirically. It does not say he cared more about machine learning’s research goals than theoretical computer science’s.

sol-6.1.text:
I was drawn to the mathematical side of computer science—being able to take a problem, make the assumptions precise, and understand why a solution works. Machine learning offered a lot of that same intellectual appeal, but with this additional question of how the theory connects to something you can actually train and use.

That gap was really interesting to me. You have these relatively simple mathematical descriptions of models, but their behavior can be surprisingly difficult to explain. I wanted to understand that better, and to see whether mathematical insights could help us design better methods.

r001.rationale: The response says machine learning shared theoretical computer science’s intellectual appeal and adds interest in connecting theory to trainable, usable methods. It does not attribute the shift to caring more about machine learning’s research goals than theoretical computer science’s.
